svg.title: Browser vs Machine vs Agent: three callers, three ways to fail
svg.desc: Three kinds of caller reach the same endpoint: a browser (a person and every script on the page), a machine (a service account with no person behind it) and an AI agent (a model choosing tools for a person). Each card shows who calls, how identity is proven, how consent arrives, what limits it, and its gaps. Arrows meet at one endpoint that must ask which kind of caller it is and apply that caller's rule. A table compares how each fails open, what replay looks like, where data leaks, where consent is checked and what an audit must answer. A band traces assumptions that hold for a JVM that never leaves its VM and how each breaks when you add commerce, go global, and add LLMs that make the system AI-legible. Seventeen lettered gaps, B1 to B5, M1 to M5 and A1 to A7, each have a fix.
svg.text: BROWSER vs MACHINE vs AGENT — THREE CALLERS, THREE WAYS TO FAIL
who is calling, what proves it, what limits it, and where each one breaks
Dashed = a gap. B = browser, M = machine, A = agent. Numbers match the list below.
THREE CALLERS, ONE ENDPOINT — THE SAME API CAN'T TRUST THEM THE SAME WAY
a person, through a user agent you don't control
A person, plus every script on the page
Session cookie, OAuth or passkey login
A banner choice: Consent Mode v2 signals
Same-origin policy, CSP, SameSite cookies, CORS
Client checks are suggestions: anyone edits the JS
Third-party tags see everything on the page
Tokens in localStorage are readable by any XSS
Tags fire before the consent choice lands
Hydrated props ship data into the HTML
a service calling a service: webhooks, cron, ETL, iPaaS
A service account, often with no person behind it
API key, HMAC signature, mTLS or client credentials
Nothing, unless the record carries it as data
Scopes, network policy, allowlists, rate limits
No person in the loop: the job runs with full power
Consent drops out of the record in transforms
Queues and logs keep the payload
an AI acting for a person: MCP tools, agentic checkout
A model choosing tools, for a user who isn't watching
A delegated token plus a signed mandate (AP2)
A mandate per action: what, how much, until when
Tool allowlist, mandate check, budget, approval
Excessive agency: tools broader than the task
Token passthrough: the agent forwards your token
Mandate replay, or scope drift past the mandate
Exfiltration through a tool call or a URL
Same prompt, different action: retries double-spend
No record of why the agent acted
Your endpoint: Cloudflare Worker · Xano · API
First ask which kind of caller this is, then apply that caller's rule. One rule for all three fails all three.
a user session, CSRF protection, and server-side authorization per record
a verified signature or mTLS, a narrow scope, and an idempotency key
the user AND the agent identified, a valid mandate, an allowed tool, and an audit entry
A check lives only in client JavaScript
A key outlives its job or its scope
Tool output is read as an instruction
A resubmitted form or a stolen session
A redelivered webhook or a re-run batch
A retried tool call or a reused mandate
On every record, as a field
Before every side effect, as a mandate
Which key, which job, which payload?
Which user, agent, mandate and tool, and why?
ASSUMPTIONS THAT BREAK AS YOU GROW — FROM A JVM THAT NEVER LEAVES THE VM TO A SYSTEM AI CAN READ
A JVM THAT NEVER LEAVES THE VM
The VM is the wall; inside is trusted
Payments, tax and tag scripts run outside it
Clouds and regions multiply the walls
Your content is input to someone else's model
One app, one user table, one session store
Local logins and age rules per market
An agent acts for a user: identify both
In the heap and one database
Card data enters PCI scope; webhooks leave
Residency: where each copy lives is legal
Prompts, embeddings and model logs are copies
Not modeled: the app owns its data
Marketing consent and order data diverge
GDPR, CPRA, PIPA, CASL: defaults differ
Training and retrieval need their own yes
One clock, one currency, one locale
Retries and refunds need idempotency keys
Currencies, tax, FX, time zones, languages
An agent can spend: mandate, amount, expiry
An exception stays in the log
A failure can charge twice or lose an order
One region down mustn't take the others
A plausible wrong answer looks like success
Who paid, refunded or changed a price?
Which law applied, and where did data go?
Which user, agent, mandate and source?
Auditors, the PCI assessor, payment partners
Each column keeps every problem to its left. The AI column is dashed: making a system legible to machines also makes it readable, quotable and steerable by them.
SEVENTEEN GAPS — AND THE CONTROL THAT CLOSES EACH
Fix: Authorize every request on the server, per record
Fix: CSP, Subresource Integrity, a script inventory (PCI DSS 6.4.3)
Fix: HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies; nothing in localStorage
Fix: Consent Mode default denied; load tags after the choice
Fix: Pass only what the screen shows; fetch PII after consent
Fix: Least-privilege scopes, short lifetimes, rotation
Fix: Act as a named service, log it, cap what it can change
Fix: Carry consent state as a field; refuse records without it
Fix: Verify the HMAC on the raw body; one idempotency key per event
Fix: Store IDs, not payloads; purge queues; scrub logs
Fix: Treat fetched content as data; approve side effects outside the model
Fix: One narrow tool per task; read and write as separate tools
Fix: Audience-bound tokens per tool; never forward the user's token
Fix: Sign amount, merchant, expiry and nonce; check every call
Fix: Egress allowlist; no raw-URL tools; filter outputs for PII
Fix: An idempotency key on every side-effecting tool call
Fix: Log user, agent, mandate, tool and inputs to an append-only ledger
A browser is a person whose code you can't trust. A machine is code with no person. An agent is code choosing what to do for a person. Each needs its own rule at the same endpoint.
